Commentary of Sayyid Qutb, *Fi Zilal al-Quran* (Urdu translation), on Surah 96, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging clot. Read, and your Lord is most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know.﴾ (96:1–4)

The Messenger (ﷺ) returned with this revelation (*wahy*, divine revelation), and he was trembling. He came to Khadijah (RA) and said, "Cover me, cover me." So she covered him with a cloak, until his fear departed. Then he said to Khadijah, "What has happened to me?" and he related the whole account to her, and said, "I feared that I might lose my life." Khadijah (RA) replied, "Never! I give you glad tidings. By Allah, Allah will never leave you desolate. You uphold the ties of kinship, you speak the truth, you help the weak, you host guests, and you assist others in the hardships of the truth."

Then Khadijah (RA) took him to her paternal cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal ibn Asad ibn Abd al-Uzza ibn Qusayy. Waraqah had become a Christian in the Days of Ignorance (*Jahiliyyah*), and he used to write the Injil in Hebrew and Arabic, as much as Allah willed. At that time he was very old and blind. Khadijah (RA) said to him, "Brother, listen to what your nephew has to say." Waraqah said, "Nephew, what did you see?" So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related what he had seen. Waraqah then said, "This is the same angel who descended upon Musa (peace be upon him). Would that I were young, and would that I were alive when your people expel you." The Messenger (ﷺ) said, "Will they truly expel me from my homeland?" Waraqah said, "Whoever has brought a teaching like what you have brought has been met with enmity. If I live to see your day, I will surely help you." Not long passed before Waraqah died.

(This hadith is narrated by Imam al-Zuhri in Bukhari and Muslim.)

Tabari has related from Abdullah ibn Zubayr: "…Jibril came to me with a piece of brocade, while I was sleeping. In it was a book. He said to me, 'Read.' I said, 'I cannot read.' Then he squeezed me so tightly that I thought my life had departed. Then he released me and said, 'Read.' I said, 'What shall I read?' I said this out of fear that the angel would again do to me what he had done. He then said:

﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created…what he did not know﴾ (96:1–5).

The Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'Then I read it. I read it to the end. I read it to the end.' After that, the angel left me, and I awoke from my sleep. The condition was that a book had been inscribed upon my heart." The Messenger (ﷺ) said that among all of God's creatures, poets and madmen were the most hateful to him; he could not even look at these two kinds of people. He said, "I thought that death was better than being a poet or a madman, so that the Quraysh could not use the words 'poet' or 'madman' about me. It would be better for me to climb a high mountain, throw myself from it, and kill myself, and thus be freed from this situation." So I set out with this intention, until I was in the middle of the mountain, when I heard a voice from the sky saying, 'O Muhammad (ﷺ), you are the Messenger of Allah, and I am Jibril.' I raised my head toward the sky, and behold, Jibril was standing on the horizon of the sky in human form, saying, 'O Muhammad (ﷺ), you are the Messenger of Allah, and I am Jibril.'" He said, "I stood still and kept looking at him, and that sight stopped me from doing what I had wanted to do. I could neither advance a step nor turn back. I tried to turn my face away from him toward the horizons of the sky, but wherever I looked, I found him standing there. So I remained standing, neither advancing a step nor retreating a step, until Khadijah sent her men to search for me. They reached Makkah, saw me, and returned to Khadijah. I remained standing there. Then he (Jibril) departed, and I too returned to Makkah to my family." Ibn Ishaq has also narrated this report in a longer form from Wahb ibn Kaysan.

I have reflected deeply on this event. We had read this first event many times in the books of Sirah, and we had seen it in the books of tafsir as well, but we had passed on after reading it, or after reflecting on it only briefly. Yet, on reflection now, it becomes clear that this was a great event, indeed a most momentous one. However much we imagine its greatness, some of its aspects will still remain beyond our imagination. In any case, this event is great both in its reality and in its meaning. It is great in the effects it produced on human life, and the moments in which it occurred were among the most precious and great moments of this earth, from the beginning of the order of the universe until its end.

The question is: what was this event, and what took place in those moments? The reality is this: Allah, Glorified is He, who is Most Great, Compelling, Supreme, and the Sovereign of the Kingdom, cast His gracious gaze from His lofty heights upon that reality which, in common usage, is called "man," who lay in a obscure corner of Allah's great universe, which in common usage is called "earth." Allah bestowed upon this creature, man, the honor of becoming the locus of divine manifestations, the trustee of Allah's wisdom, and the recipient of Allah's word, and thus he became an example of the station and rank to which Allah's decree and plan wished to elevate this creature.

This is a great matter, so great that its greatness has no limits, and its greatness becomes even clearer when a human being considers the narrowness of his own faculties. On one side is the reality of divinity, which is unrestricted, eternal, and everlasting; on the other side is a reality which is the reality of servitude, limited, changing, and perishing. Then man truly comes to realize how immense Allah's favor upon this creature was. Then he feels how great and joyful this reality is, and then he receives it with utmost humility, submission, gratitude, and happiness. Then he finds the words of Allah resounding through the boundless expanses of this universe, that these words descend upon this insignificant human being, in this insignificant dwelling. This human being is a mere speck, and this earth is a contemptible speck.

Moreover, how far-reaching are the meanings of this great event? If viewed from Allah's side, it is an expansive grace and kindness from Him. He is the Bestower of grace; within His mercy this human being is immersed; He is most generous, loving, and benevolent. When He bestows grace upon anyone, He does so without any cause or reason. This grace belongs to the aspect of His own attributes.

If viewed from the perspective of man, Allah has bestowed upon man a favor beyond what he could ever imagine, and now he cannot give thanks for it. Even if all of humanity were to give thanks for this single act of kindness alone, and even if they remained in bowing and prostration day and night, still the right of this one act of kindness could not be fulfilled. This is the kindness that Allah remembers His servant, casts His gracious gaze upon him, establishes a connection with him, and sends a noble personality from among human beings as a Messenger. The earth becomes the place of descent for Allah's words, the dwelling of this Messenger becomes a station, and the echo of these words rises across the regions and surroundings of this earth.

As for what change occurred in the life of all humanity as a result of this event, the fact is that from the very first moment its effects began to touch humanity. The course of history changed; the contours of the human conscience were altered; the qibla was fixed, toward which man was to turn, and from which people were to derive their concepts and standards of values. These standards were not earthly or material, but heavenly standards drawn from divine revelation.

From that time until today, those people in whose souls this truth settled entered into Allah's mercy and compassion; Allah's mercy began to fall upon them directly. Their attitude became such that in every matter, whether small or great, they kept their eyes directly fixed upon Allah. These people moved under Allah's gaze. They hoped that Allah would support them, guide them step by step toward their destination, prevent them from a wrong path, and turn them toward the right path. And they always hoped that revelation would come at any moment and unveil the secrets of their hearts. They expected that a command from Allah would come at any moment and resolve their difficulties, telling them to do this and to refrain from that.

The truth is that this was a remarkable era; this was an era of twenty-three years. During these times, a direct relationship was established between human beings and their Lord. It was an era that only those who lived within it could truly understand: those who felt it, who witnessed its beginning and its end, who experienced the sweetness of this direct connection, and who perceived that the hand of divine power was supporting them at every step. They saw from where they had set out and where they had arrived. It was a journey, a revolutionary journey, whose length could not be measured by any standard of this world. It was a journey of the human conscience, which cannot be measured by the distances of the cosmos. It was not even a journey between two celestial bodies; rather, it was a complete transformation and revolution. Now, in place of material and earthly standards, heavenly standards had come; instead of seeking help from desires, they were now seeking help from revelation. People had journeyed from Jahiliyyah into Islam; from polytheism they had entered into the realm of godliness (*rabbaniyyah*). It was a long journey, longer and more distant than the distance between the earth and the heavens.

These people possessed a taste for knowledge of God (*ma'rifah*), they tasted its sweetness and savor, they were aware of its value, and when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away, they felt its absence. They realized that an era had come to an end. Had this era not truly passed, the intellect could not even have imagined it.

It is related from Anas (RA) that after the death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr (RA) said to Umar (RA), "Come, let us visit Umm Ayman. Let us meet her in the same way that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to visit her." When they went to her, she began to weep. They asked her, "What is the reason for your weeping? Do you not know that what Allah has prepared for the Messenger of Allah is better?" She said, "Yes, I know that what Allah has prepared for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is far better, but I am weeping because revelation from the heavens has ceased." Her words moved both of them to tears, and they too began to weep. (Muslim)

This was a blessed moment, and its effects have influenced human life from that time until today, and these effects will continue to operate until Allah inherits the earth and the Day of Resurrection is established. The truth is that the event of that moment gave human beings a new life. It did so in such a way that humanity began to derive its values from heaven rather than from the earth, and to draw the system of its life from revelation, rather than from carnal desires.

What took place in that moment transformed the course of history. Before this, no such revolution had occurred in history, and nothing of this kind has happened after him. This event was truly the crossroads of history. It turned the direction of history, and then landmarks were established in history that have not been erased to this day. Subsequent events have not diminished the vividness of these landmarks. A vision of this universe, of life, and of its lofty values was established in human beliefs and ideas. These were made so clear that, before this, history had not displayed these lofty values in such a manner. This was a portrayal of lofty values that was comprehensive, pure, utterly abstract, and free and pure from the colors of the world; yet its colors were real and harmonized well with human life. Thus, the principles and foundations of the Islamic system of life were laid down, and the marks and contours of the Islamic order were established.

﴿So that whoever perishes may perish by clear proof, and whoever lives may live by clear proof.﴾ (8:42)

No ambiguity or vagueness was left in these contours. If anyone does not accept them, then he will not accept them while knowing and understanding. Now, if anyone strays from the straight path, he will do so deliberately, and if anyone adopts crookedness, he will do so intentionally.

Within this scene and this moment, this was an outstanding event. It was a cosmic occurrence which ended an age that vanished from the world, and began an age that will last forever.

This event became a *furqan* (criterion distinguishing truth from falsehood) in human history. It became a *furqan* in human life, not merely in the life of a particular nation or community. The echo of this event was recorded throughout the entire universe, and the whole universe began to move along with it. This event was recorded in the human conscience. The human conscience still remembers it today; it keeps its memories alive and never forgets it, and the human conscience recognizes that this event was, in reality, a new birth for humanity, and that this revolution in human values occurred only once in history, and there is no other example of it.

This was the matter concerning the first paragraph of this surah. As for the verses and paragraphs that follow, it is obvious that they were revealed later. The later verses point to events from the Sirah (biography) of the Prophet ﷺ that occurred in much later periods, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was commanded to preach openly, and at that time opposition to him had begun again, as will be seen. ﴿Have you seen ... the one who forbids a servant from praying?﴾ But although these were revealed later, there is a connection among the parts of the surah, and among the truths presented after the opening, there is complete order. Thus the whole surah becomes a perfect unity and a complete theme, whose parts are interwoven and organized.

﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging clot. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know.﴾ This is the first surah of the Qur'an. What was the first command given to the Messenger of Allah? What was the first guidance given? At the moments when his connection with the higher realm was first established, when he was first entrusted with the responsibility of the Islamic call, the command was: "Read in the name of your Lord who created." The attribute of creation was taken from among Allah's attributes, through which the entire universe was brought into existence from non-existence.

After this, the reality of human creation and the beginning of the human era in this universe is taken up.

"He created man from a clot of blood" (96:2): from a single drop of blood, which was static and clung to the walls of the womb. This was the starting point of human birth, whose structure is very simple. Two things come from this manner of creation: first, that Allah is most generous, and second, that His power is itself evident from His creation. The generosity lies in this: that He raised this clotted drop of blood, this microscopic point, to the station of a human being who reads and teaches.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 96, verses 3–4:

اقرا وربک ............................ مالم یعلم (96:3 to 5): "Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know."

After the creation of man, this was a very great change in him. But it is possible; He is the Most Generous. Therefore Allah brought about this change in a microscopic point, so that after being an ignorant man he became a man of knowledge. This is so great a change that one's head spins at it.

Besides this, these verses also clarify the Islamic theory of education. The Lord gave man education through the "pen." Because at that time and today too, the pen is an important and effective means of education in human life, and this reality was not understood at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an in the way we understand it today. But Allah, the Exalted, understood well the value of education and the pen. Therefore, while entrusting the last Messenger with the final mission, Allah pointed to this reality, and this indication was made in the first Surah of the Qur'an. Despite the fact that the Messenger to whom this guidance was given could not write a letter. Therefore, if anyone says that this Qur'an is the composition of a human being, no unlettered (ummi) human being could do such a thing. Therefore this is a reality that divine revelation told, and this is proof that the Messenger of God, ﷺ, is a true Messenger.

After this it is stated what the source of education is according to the Qur'an's view. This source is the Divine Being. Whatever knowledge man has acquired until today or will acquire in the future, the secrets of this universe that have been revealed to man until today have been revealed by the grace and bounty of Allah alone. The secrets of human life and the human soul that have been revealed are also revealed by the grace and bounty of Allah. Allah alone is the true source and fountainhead, besides which there is no other source of knowledge and wisdom.

This paragraph, which was revealed at the beginning of those moments in which for the first time contact was established between the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the higher realm, states within this single paragraph the fundamental principles of the faith-based conception of life, so that "every command, every movement, every step, every action and every task will be in accordance with the name of Allah and the commands of Allah; action will be taken in the name of Allah, will proceed in the name of Allah, will turn toward Allah, and its final end will reach Allah." Because Allah alone is the Creator, He is the Knower and the Giver of knowledge; from Him is the beginning, from Him is the growth, and from Him is education and training. Man learns, and what he learns he knows, and whatever he knows, yet all knowledge and skill has its source in the Divine Being who created, gave the means of knowledge, and

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 96, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):

"He taught man what he did not know" (96:5). Thus the heart of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) grasped this truth in the very first moments of the revelation from the higher realm, and this awareness pervaded his thinking, his conduct, his speech, his actions, his direction and his entire life, because it was the first principle of faith.

Imam Shams al-Din Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyyah, in his book "Zad al-Ma'ad fi Hadi Khayr al-'Ibad," says the following about the important features of the Messenger's (ﷺ) life:

"In the matter of the remembrance of Allah and His dhikr, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was an extremely complete human being. The major part of his speech consisted of matters relating to the remembrance of Allah and the Divine Being. His commands, his prohibitions, the explanation of Islamic laws, and all other instructions were in fact aspects of the remembrance of Allah. Describing the names and attributes of Allah, explaining the commands of Allah and the matters of the Shariah, warning against evil consequences and so on, were all the remembrance of Allah. Then, praising Allah for His blessings, His exaltedness, His praise and His glorification was indeed the remembrance of Allah. Then, asking from Allah, supplicating, turning towards Allah, fearing Allah, these were all different forms of the remembrance of Allah. When he was silent, he too remembered Allah. At all times and in every state, the Divine Being was present in his consciousness. With every breath that went in or came out, whether he was standing or sitting, walking or riding, on a journey or at home, residing or departing, in short, at all times and in every state he remembered Allah."

When he (ﷺ) woke from sleep, he would say:

"Al-hamdu lillahi alladhi ............................ al-nushur" — "Praise be to Allah, who gave us life after He had caused us to die (sleep), and to Him is the resurrection."

Hadrat Aishah (RA) said that whenever he (ﷺ) woke suddenly during the night, he would say "Allahu Akbar" ten times and recite the tahlil ten times, that is, he would say:

"La ilaha illallah" — "There is no ruler except Allah." Then after this he would recite this supplication ten times:

"Allahumma inni a'udhu bika min dayq al-dunya wa min dayq yawm al-qiyamah" — "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the constriction of this world and from the constriction of the Day of Resurrection." After this he would begin the prayer.

She also said that when the Messenger (ﷺ) woke during the night, he would recite this supplication:

"La ilaha illa anta, subhanaka, Allahumma astaghfiruka li-dhanbi wa as'aluka rahmataka. Allahumma zidni 'ilman wa la tuzigh qalbi ba'da idh hadaytani wa hab li min ladunka rahmatan innaka antal-Wahhab" (Abu Dawud) — "O Allah, there is no ruler but You, You are pure and exalted. O Allah, I seek forgiveness from You for my sins, and I ask You for Your mercy. O Allah, increase my knowledge and do not make my heart deviate after You have guided me, and grant me mercy from Yourself. Indeed You are the Bestower."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also said: whoever wakes at night and says:

"La ilaha illallahu wahdahu la sharika lah, lahu al-mulku wa lahu al-hamdu wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir. Al-hamdu lillahi wa subhana Allahi wa la ilaha illallahu wallahu akbar wa la hawla wa la quwwata illa billahi al-'Aliyyi al-'Azim" — "There is no ruler but Allah, He alone, having no partner. To Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is over all things powerful. All praise is for Allah, glory is to Allah, there is no ruler but Allah, Allah is Greatest, and there is no power and no strength except through Allah, the Exalted, the Mighty," and then supplicates, saying: "Allahumma-ghfir li" — "O Allah, forgive me," or any other supplication, that supplication will be accepted, and if he performs wudu and then prays, his prayer will be accepted (Bukhari).

Once Hadrat Ibn Abbas (RA) spent a night with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He says that when he woke from sleep, he raised his head towards the sky and recited the ten verses beginning "Inna fi khalqi as-samawati..." to the end, and then praised Allah in this manner:

"Allahumma laka ahmad, anta nur as-samawati wa al-ard wa man fihinna. Laka al-hamd, anta qayyim as-samawati wa al-ard wa man fihinna. Wa laka al-hamd, anta al-haqq, wa wa'duka al-haqq, wa qawluka al-haqq, wa liqa'uka al-haqq, wa al-jannatu haqq, wa al-nar haqq, wa al-nabiyyuna haqq, wa Muhammadun haqq, wa al-sa'atu haqq. Allahumma laka aslamtu wa bika amantu wa 'alayka tawakkaltu wa ilayka anabtu wa bika khasamtu wa ilayka hakamtu, faghfir li ma qaddamtu wa ma akhkhartu wa ma asrartu wa ma a'lantu, anta ilahi, la ilaha illa anta wa la hawla wa la quwwata illa billahi al-'Aliyyi al-'Azim."

"O Allah, all praise is for You. You are the light of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them. All praise is for You. You are the sustainer of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them. And all praise is for You. You are the Truth, Your promise is true, Your word is true, meeting You is true, Paradise is true, Hell is true, the prophets are true, Muhammad is true, and the Hour is true. O Allah, I have submitted to You, I have believed in You, I have relied upon You, I have turned to You, I have disputed by Your help, and I have brought my affairs before You for judgement. So forgive me for what I have done before and what I have left behind, what I have concealed and what I have made public. You are my God, there is no ruler but You, and there is no power and no strength except through Allah, the Exalted, the Mighty."

Hadrat Aishah (RA) said that when the Messenger (ﷺ) stood in prayer at night, he would recite this supplication:

"Allahumma rabba Jibra'il wa Mika'il wa Israfil, fatira as-samawati wa al-ard, 'alima al-ghaybi wa al-shahadah, anta tahkumu bayna 'ibadika fima kanu fihi yakhtalifun. Ihdini lima ikhtulifa fihi mina al-haqqi bi-idhnika, innaka tahdi man tasha'u ila sirat mustaqim."

"O Allah, Lord of Jibril, Mikail and Israfil, Creator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the visible, You judge between Your servants concerning that in which they differ. Guide me, by Your permission, to the truth in matters over which they have differed, for indeed You guide whom You will to the straight path." He (the narrator) said that presumably he said that the Messenger (ﷺ) began his prayer with this supplication.

When he (ﷺ) offered witr, after finishing the witr he would recite "Subhan al-Malik al-Quddus" three times, and the third time he would recite it aloud, drawing out the voice.

When he (ﷺ) left his house, he would recite this supplication:

"Bismillah, tawakkaltu 'ala Allah. Allahumma inni a'udhu bika min an adilla aw udalla, aw azilla aw uzalla, aw azlima aw uzlama, aw ajhala aw yujhala 'alayya" (Hadith sahih) — "In the name of Allah, I have relied upon Allah. O Allah, I seek refuge in You from going astray or being led astray, from slipping or being made to slip, from wronging or being wronged, from acting ignorantly or being treated ignorantly."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said that whoever leaves his house and recites this supplication:

"Bismillah, tawakkaltu 'ala Allah, wa la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah" — "I begin in the name of Allah, I have relied upon Allah, and there is no power and no strength except with Allah." Then it is said to such a person by Allah: "You have been guided, your needs have been met, and you have been protected" (or "you have been given full reward"), and the devil will withdraw from him (Hadith hasan).

Once Hadrat Ibn Abbas (RA) stayed with him for a night. He says that in the morning, when the Messenger (ﷺ) went out for prayer, he recited this supplication:

"Allahumma-j'al qalbi nuran, wa-j'al fi lisani nuran, wa-j'al fi sam'i nuran, wa-j'al fi basari nuran, wa-j'al min khalfi nuran, wa min amami nuran, wa-j'al min fawqi nuran, wa-j'al min tahti nuran. Allahumma a'zim li nuran."

"O Allah, place light in my heart, place light on my tongue, place light in my hearing, place light in my sight, place light behind me and before me, place light above me and below me. O Allah, magnify my light for me."

Fadl ibn Marzuq has narrated from Atiyyah al-Awfi, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: whoever leaves his house for prayer and recites this supplication:

"Allahumma inni as'aluka bi-haqqi as-sa'ilina 'alayka, wa bi-haqqi mamshaya ilayka. Fa-inni lam akhruj ashiran wa la atiyan wa la riya'an wa la sum'atan, wa innama kharajtu ittiqa'a sakhatika wa ibtighaa' mardatika, as'aluka an tunqidhani mina an-nar wa an taghfira li dhunubi, fa-innahu la yaghfiru adh-dhunuba illa anta" — "O Allah, I ask You by the right of those who ask You, and by the right of my walking towards You. For I have not gone out in pride or arrogance, nor for show or reputation, but I have gone out to guard against Your wrath and to seek Your pleasure. I ask You to save me from the Fire and to forgive my sins, for none forgives sins but You" — Allah will appoint seventy thousand angels who will seek forgiveness for him, and Allah will turn His blessed face towards him as long as he does not finish the prayer (this hadith is weak both in its chain and its text).

Imam Abu Dawud has narrated that whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the mosque, he would say:

"A'udhu billahi al-'Azim, wa bi-wajhihi al-Karim, wa sultanihi al-Qadim, min ash-shaytan ar-rajim" — "I seek refuge in Allah the Mighty, in His noble face and in His ancient authority, from the accursed Satan." When someone recites this supplication, Satan says that this person has protected himself from me for the entire day.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When any one of you enters the mosque, he should send blessings and peace upon me, and then recite this supplication:

"Allahumma-ftah li abwaba rahmatik" — "O Allah, open for me the doors of Your mercy." And when he leaves the mosque, he should say: "Allahumma inni as'aluka min fadlik" — "O Allah, I ask You for Your bounty."

It is also reported from him that whenever he entered the mosque he would send blessings and peace upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, and then say: "Allahumma-ghfir li dhunubi wa-ftah li abwaba rahmatik" — "O Allah, forgive my sins and open for me the doors of Your mercy." And when he went out, he would again send blessings and peace upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, and then say: "Allahumma-ghfir li dhunubi wa-ftah li bab rahmatik" — "O Allah, forgive my sins and open for me the door of Your bounty."

It was the custom of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that when he had prayed the morning prayer, he would sit at his prayer place remembering Allah until the sun rose. When morning came, he would say:

"Allahumma bika asbahna, wa bika amsayna, wa bika nahya, wa bika namutu, wa ilayka an-nushur" (Hadith sahih) — "O Allah, by Your command we reach the morning, and by Your command we reach the evening, by Your command we live, by Your command we die, and to You is the resurrection."

He also used to say these words:

"Asbahna wa asbaha al-mulku lillah, wal-hamdu lillah, la ilaha illallahu wahdahu la sharika lah, lahu al-mulku wa lahu al-hamdu wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir. Rabbi as'aluka khayra ma fi hadhal-yawm wa khayra ma ba'dahu, wa a'udhu bika min sharri hadhal-yawm wa sharri ma ba'dahu. Rabbi a'udhu bika min al-kasali wa su'il-kibar. Rabbi a'udhu bika min 'adhabin fin-nar wa 'adhabin fil-qabr" — "We have entered the morning, and all sovereignty belongs to Allah, all praise belongs to Allah, there is no ruler but Allah, He alone, without partner. To Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is powerful over all things. O Lord, I ask You for the good of this day and the good of what follows it, and I seek refuge in You from the evil of this day and the evil of what follows it. O Lord, I seek refuge in You from laziness and the evils of old age. O Lord, I seek refuge in You from the punishment of the Fire and the punishment of the grave."

When evening came, he would recite this same supplication in the form: "Amsayna wa amsa al-mulku ba'd..." — "We have reached the evening, and sovereignty belongs to Allah..." to the end (Muslim).

Hadrat Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA) asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to teach him words which he might say in the morning and evening. He (ﷺ) said that he should say these words:

"Allahumma fatira as-samawati wa al-ard, 'alima al-ghaybi wa ash-shahadah, rabba kulli shay'in wa malikahu, ashhadu an la ilaha illa anta. A'udhu bika min sharri nafsi wa sharri ash-shaytani wa shirkihi, wa an aqtarifa 'ala nafsi su'an aw ajurrahu ila muslim" (Muslim) — "O Creator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the visible, Lord and Sovereign of all things, I bear witness that there is no god but You. I seek refuge in You from the evil of my soul and the evil of Satan and his partnership, and from committing evil against myself or bringing harm upon a Muslim."

After this, he related many traditions on this subject.

And when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wore a new garment, he would mention it by name, that is, trousers, shirt or cloak, and then recite:

"Allahumma laka al-hamd, anta kasawtanihi, as'aluka khayrahu wa khayra ma suni'a lahu, wa a'udhu bika min sharrihi wa sharri ma suni'a lahu" (Hadith sahih) — "O Allah, all praise is for You. You have clothed me with it. I ask You for its good and the good of that for which it was made, and I seek refuge in You from its evil and the evil of that for which it was made."

It is also reported from him that when he returned to his home, he would recite this supplication:

"Al-hamdu lillahi alladhi kafani wa awani, wal-hamdu lillahi alladhi at'amani wa saqani, wal-hamdu lillahi alladhi mann 'alayya. As'aluka an tujirani mina an-nar" — "Praise be to Allah who has sufficed me and given me shelter. Praise be to Allah who has fed me and given me drink. Praise be to Allah who has bestowed favour upon me. I ask You to protect me from the Fire."

And in the Sahihayn it is narrated that when he went to the toilet, he would say:

"Allahumma inni a'udhu bika min al-khubthi wal-khaba'ith" — "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from evil things and evil beings" (male and female devils). And when he came out of the toilet, he would say: "Ghufranaka" — "I seek Your forgiveness." And it is also reported that he would say these words:

"Al-hamdu lillahi alladhi adhhaba 'anni al-adha wa 'afani" — "Praise be to Allah who has removed harm from me and granted me well-being."

"Praise be to Allah, who has removed from me that which is harmful and granted me well-being." (Ibn Majah)

It is also established from you (ﷺ) that you placed your blessed hand into a vessel containing water, and then said to the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them): "Make wudu' in the name of Allah."

It is also narrated from you (ﷺ) that when you saw the moon you would recite this supplication:

"Allahumma ahillahu 'alaina bil-amni wal-iman, was-salamati wal-Islam. Rabbi wa Rabbuka Allah."

"O Allah, bring this moon up over us with security, faith, safety and Islam. O moon, my Lord and your Lord is Allah." (Tirmidhi)

And when you would put your hand into food, you would say Bismillah, and you would instruct the people to say Bismillah and eat. You would say: when any of you eats, let him mention the name of Allah. If he forgets and is unable to say it at the beginning, then let him say:

"Bismillahi fi awwalihi wa akhirihi."

"In the name of Allah at its beginning and at its end." (Sahih)

This was the life of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and throughout this entire life you acted upon the guidance that was given at the beginning of the revelation. This principle had become deeply rooted in your faith, your convictions, and your actions and movements.

The requirement of this reality would have been that a person should attain recognition of Allah and give thanks to Allah, that is, for the fact that Allah created him, taught him knowledge, and made him honoured among all creation. But man did not do so; rather, he went in the exact opposite direction, and his deviation and his unexpected conduct are mentioned in the next paragraph.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 96, verses 6–7:

Man does not reflect that it is Allah alone who gives him and makes him self-sufficient. Before this, it was Allah who created him, made him honoured above all creatures, and gave him knowledge. Yet man's general attitude is that when he is given and made self-sufficient, he generally does not render thanks to his Lord, unless Allah protects someone's faith from this ingratitude. Commonly it happens that man is not even aware of the source from which this giving and self-sufficiency are coming, although the One who gives and makes him self-sufficient is the same One who created him, bestowed honour upon him and gave him knowledge. But man not only fails to be sensitive to this Benefactor; rather, he adopts the path of extreme rebellion, depravity and wickedness, he revolts and he becomes arrogant, whereas his duty was to recognise Allah's favours and be thankful.

This is a portrait of a rebellious human being who has forgotten even his own creation, and whom wealth-worship has greatly corrupted. Thus a threat is given to him in an oblique and indirect manner.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 96, verse 8:

Inna ilā Rabbika al-rujʿā (96:8): "Surely, to your Lord is the return." Where, then, will this heedless and rebellious one flee? In the end, the coming back is to Allah alone.

But alongside this warning, a fundamental principle and conception of the Islamic worldview is also presented: that all must present themselves in the court of Allah. All must return to Allah, in every matter, in every respect, in every intention and resolve, and in every deed and movement, for there is no refuge and no place of return other than Allah. Whether one is righteous or wicked, all must go before Allah. Whether one is obedient or given to disobedience, whether one is upon the truth or upon falsehood, whether one is good or mischievous, whether one is rich or poor, all must go before Allah alone. The person who, considering himself self-sufficient, transgressed, will also find himself bound before Allah. Therefore, every person should prepare something for the time of presenting himself before Allah, because He is the Creator and to Him is the return.

In this way, these two paragraphs take up both ends of Islamic beliefs and doctrines: the Islamic view of the beginning and growth of life, then the Islamic view of education, training, refinement and civility, and then the return to Allah, the belief in resurrection, gathering and reckoning, and going before Allah for judgment, where all authority will belong to Allah.

Inna ilā Rabbika al-rujʿā (96:8): "Surely, to your Lord is the return."

Now the third paragraph comes. The surah is very brief, yet here rebellion is depicted in a very clear and hideous portrayal. The human being is left astonished and strongly disapproves of such incidents. This depiction is in the unique style of the Qur'an.

Qur'an presents this scene in an extremely repugnant form, yet in a most clear manner. The style of the Qur'an is its own, and no writer can give it a written style. It is a living and radiant oratorical style, in which it is presented in the form of very brief glimpses, with great ease and lightness, and in the form of a very swift-moving film.

"Ara'ayta" (ارءیت): "Have you seen?" Such a repugnant scene has also at some time passed before your eyes. Can you believe that such a thing could also happen?

"Ara'ayta ... (al-ladhi yanha) ... Salla" (10:96): "Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays?" Do you not see how evil and shameful an act this is? It is a most repugnant act that one person is worshipping God and another is preventing him from worshipping. Furthermore, the situation is that the former is upon the right guidance, and is giving people guidance to piety, God-fearing and good things, while the one who forbids is forbidding him.

Then, over and above this, he is committing this act, a most sinful act, and along with it he is committing an act even worse than it.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 96, verse 13:

"Have you considered, if he denies and turns away?" (96:13) Here too, an indirect and veiled threat is given, just as it was given at the end of the previous paragraph.

Alif Lam Mim ........................ "Does he not know that Allah sees?" (96:14). Allah sees that this man is denying the truth without cause, turning away without cause, and that this servant (of the Lord), who is a believer... no, rather, this man stops the Prophet (ﷺ) from prayer without cause, while the Prophet (ﷺ) is upon guidance, enjoins righteousness (taqwa), and looks toward the Hereafter.

Alif Lam Mim ........................ "Does he not know that Allah sees?" (96:14). This is a scene in which a person stands in the way of the Islamic call, blocking the path of faith and blocking the path of obedience and God-consciousness (taqwa). Such a person is now given a final threat, and it is an open threat, without any concealment.

This is a clear and direct threat, and it is expressed in severe words.

"Nay! If he does not desist, We will certainly seize him by the forelock (nasiyah)" (96:15). ﴿Kalla la-in lam yantahi la-nasfa'an bil-nasiyah﴾

The very pronunciation of "lanasfa'an" is harsh, and its sound also points to the severity of its meaning. Safa' means to seize forcefully. Nasiyah means the forelock, the front part of the head. The forehead is a high place for the arrogant and the proud to display their pride. Such people hold their heads high, and when the head is raised, the forehead rises with it. Therefore, it is fitting to seize such a forehead and bring it down, because

"Nasiyatin kaziba" (96:16): "a lying, sinful forelock." And since this is a place of seizing and dragging, and in such situations people call upon their friends and helpers, it is said: [then let him call his assembly, We will call the guards of hell].
(96:17) "Let him call his supporters." We too will take care of the matter.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 96, verse 18:

﴿سَنَدْعُ الزَّبَانِيَةَ﴾ "We too will call the guards of hell." They are the ones who are extremely harsh in temperament and severe in their grip. Obviously, the outcome of such a confrontation will be their humiliation.

This surah ends with this anticipated and frightening scene. On this scene, the believers are commanded to remain steadfast in their faith and Islam, and to continue obeying the commands of Allah.

This refers to the rebellious one who prevents you from prayer. Do not obey him. Resist him when he obstructs the Islamic call. Draw near to your Lord by prostrating before Him. A person draws near to God only through worship and obedience. Ignore such rebels and leave them to the powers of Allah to deal with them.

According to authentic narrations, apart from the first paragraph of this surah, the rest of it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. When he came to the Kaaba, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was praying at the Maqam Ibrahim (the Station of Ibrahim, the stone near the Kaaba where Ibrahim stood while building it). He said, "O Muhammad, did I not forbid you from this?" He threatened the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) also rebuked him severely. Perhaps on this occasion the Prophet (ﷺ) seized him by the throat and said:

﴿أَوْلَىٰ لَكَ فَأَوْلَىٰ﴾ (Woe to you, and woe again; turn back, or else ....)

Abu Jahl then said, "O Muhammad, what do you threaten me with? By Allah, I have the most supporters and friends in this valley." Then this verse was revealed:

﴿فَلْيَدْعُ نَادِيَهُ﴾ (96:17) "Let him call upon his assembly." Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said that if at that time he had called his supporters, the angels of punishment would have seized him immediately.

However, the meaning of this surah is general. This surah applies to every believer and obedient caller to Allah (da'i ila Allah), and to every rebellious and disobedient opponent who stands against them. Every rebel who prevents people from prayer, forbids them from obeying Allah, and plots against righteousness is threatened by this warning. The final guidance is:

﴿كَلَّا لَا تُطِعْهُ وَاسْجُدْ وَاقْتَرِبْ﴾ (96:19) "No! Do not obey him, but prostrate yourself and draw near to Allah."

According to this interpretation, all the paragraphs of the surah become interconnected.
